transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-28
Time: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~75 minutes
Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Jordan (Redwood SE), Kim (Atlas SRE), Priya (Atlas ML), Michael (CTO), Lara (Platform), Tom (PM)

Summary (auto): Workshop to align on benchmarking methodology for runtime performance and apples-to-apples comparisons across VPC/on-prem vs hosted.

00:00 Alex (AE): hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll try to cover a reproducible benchmarking plan — prompt sets, load generation, metrics to capture, and what 'apples to apples' means here.
00:18 Jordan (SE): quick agenda: we wanna define prompt set slices (short, mid, long), token distributions, cold vs warm cache, batching concurrency, and quant profiles. also discuss network jitter inside VPCs and on prem.
00:37 Kim (SRE): great, our big worry is tail latency and consistency during spikes. we have strict p99 targets for our interactive product.
00:50 Priya (ML): and we care about regressions in output quality when applying 8-bit and 4-bit quant; we'll need eval prompts tied to f1/accuracy thresholds.
01:05 Alex: yep, so first item: prompt sets. we recommend three canonical sets: short completion (<=64 tokens), mid (65-256), long (>256). each set should include 500-2k examples representative of production. can you share logs?
01:22 Priya: yes we can anonymize logs; question: should we token-normalize? we have some multi-byte tokens in finance jargon.
01:30 Jordan: keep raw tokenization but record tokenizer and model version; apples-to-apples requires same tokenizer and model checkpoint across runs. also include seed for deterministic sampling where applicable.
01:48 Michael (CTO): when you say apples-to-apples, does that include same hardware? we expect on-prem GPUs to be slightly older.
01:56 Jordan: important point — apples-to-apples has levels: level 1 same model/checkpoint + tokenizer + config; level 2 same model + matched compute (e.g., same GPU class); level 3 identical infra. we'll capture metadata for each run so comparisons are fair.
02:12 Tom (PM): what metrics should we report? p50/p95/p99, throughput (req/s), tokens/sec, cost per 1M tokens?
02:20 Alex: all of those. also cold-start latency, warm steady-state, and cache hit rates for KV cache. include jitter and CPU/GPU utilization stats.
02:35 Kim: how do KV cache hits affect p99? our workloads have many repeated prefixes.
02:41 Jordan: KV cache can reduce tokens decoded and dramatically lower latency for repeated prefixes. benchmark both with cache cold and cache warm. important to simulate prefix distribution like production — otherwise you overestimate benefit.
02:57 Priya: any recommended way to simulate cache warm-up?
03:02 Jordan: run a warm-up phase with representative traffic for 10-30 minutes, then run the measurement window. record cache hit ratio over time. note that batching interacts: larger batch windows can hide cache benefits because you accumulate more unique prefixes.
03:21 Alex: on batching, we should test multiple batching profiles: low-latency mode (batch size small, immediate flush) and high-throughput mode (larger batch windows). measure p50/p95/p99 and tail isolates.
03:36 Michael: and quantization — do we compare float16 vs int8 vs 4-bit?
03:40 Jordan: yes. include fp16 baseline, 8-bit quant (LLM.int8 or similar), and 4-bit if available. crucial: measure both latency and output-quality using the eval prompt set. sometimes 4-bit reduces memory but increases latency for some kernels due to dequant overhead.
03:58 Lara (Platform): for VPC/on-prem differences — network latency matters, but also model compilation/kernels differ by driver versions. we saw variance when CUDA/cuDNN versions differed.
04:12 Jordan: capture driver, cuda, cuDNN, and any compiler flags. for on-prem, also note NUMA topology and inter-GPU connectivity. we'll add a host spec file to the harness.
04:28 Kim: security questions — can the benchmarking harness run inside our VPC without exfiltrating logs? we need to keep data on prem.
04:36 Alex: yes, we can provide a self-contained harness tarball that runs locally; results can be uploaded or shared via a secure S3/RSA wrapper. we also have guidance for running in an air-gapped environment — but you won't get Redwood hosted numbers in that case, only Dedicated/Private runs.
04:52 Priya: load generation — should we use constant concurrency or poisson arrivals?
04:56 Jordan: both. use poisson for realistic burstiness, and fixed concurrency to stress throughput. include ramp-up phases and hold windows (e.g., 5 min steady-state).
05:09 Tom: we need to ensure token accounting is consistent across vendors — some platforms count prompt+completion differently.
05:17 Alex: agree. record raw token counts from tokenizer and include both prompt and completion tokens. when comparing cost figures, normalize to 1M tokens of model-side tokens.
05:30 Michael: what's your suggestion for measuring model fallback and graceful degradation?
05:35 Jordan: create a mix of traffic that includes occasional heavy requests; configure fallback policy to a cheaper quantized variant or smaller model and measure error rates and latency. capture functional regression with eval prompts.
05:50 Priya: about determinism — sampling can add variance; we should use greedy/deterministic decoding for latency runs and sampling only for quality evals.
06:00 Alex: good call. metrics table in harness should include run-id, model, quant, batcher config, concurrency, seed, p50/p95/p99, throughput, tokens/sec, cache_hit_rate, gpu_util, host_cpu, net_rtt, and a link to the eval report.
06:18 Jordan: also collect profiler traces where possible (nvprof, triton traces, or our runtime trace) for kernel hotspots. these are invaluable for tuning.
06:30 Kim: there's some fuzz in transcriptions of product names in our logs — will that break tokenization?
06:36 Priya: we can pre-process but will include raw logs as well.
06:40 Jordan: one more practical: if you want apples-to-apples across vendors we should freeze the model binary (sha), and provide a small reference server that loads the same checkpoint and returns tokens vs logits so you can compare decode stacks.
06:58 Lara: okay so timeline and deliverables?
07:02 Alex: deliverables: prompt set + harness (Alex), baseline config + initial runs on Redwood Dedicated (Jordan), anonymized logs (Priya), infra spec (Kim). we'll reconvene after the baseline runs.
07:16 Tom: any blockers on our side? Kim: need to validate air-gapped infra and scheduling maintenance window for test runs.
07:26 Jordan: technical note — when reporting p99, indicate sample size and whether you're including conditional caching behavior; small sample sizes can mislead.
07:40 Alex: we'll include recommended sample sizes; aim for at least several thousand requests per slice.
07:48 Priya: question on KV cache — does Redwood's runtime expose cache eviction metrics?
07:52 Jordan: yes we can emit cache hits/misses/evictions per tenant. the harness can log those. beware that eviction patterns differ with sequence length variance.
08:08 Michael: last item: cost normalization again — if we're comparing on-prem GPU cost, should we amortize hardware + power + ops?
08:16 Alex: for internal comparison yes; we'll provide a cost model template to fill in fixed costs and ops overhead to compute $/1M tokens. for vendor hosted, use list pricing as baseline and annotate discounts.
08:30 Action recap: Alex will send harness and prompt sets; Jordan will prepare baseline config and run Dedicated experiments; Priya/Kim will share logs and infra spec; we schedule follow-up the week of 2026-06-15.
08:50 Michael: thanks, this was helpful.
08:54 Alex: thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email with attachments and the calendar invite.

End of transcript. Some transcription artifacts present: speaker overlaps, small mis-hearings ("K V cache" vs "KV cache"), and occasional punctuation drop-offs.
